title: How Many Communication Platforms Are in Use in Your Organization?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership field note argues that letting communication tools multiply across an organization is an expedient choice with a hidden long-term cost. Drawing on research on organizational silos, it claims that teams working in separate, unintegrated platforms interact less, which weakens collaboration, slows information flow and erodes alignment. Ford Motor Company serves as the case study: developers, business teams and meetings had each settled on different tools, and moving roughly 170,000 people onto one platform broke down the resulting silos. The note then explains why proliferation happens, since leaders approve each tool on the basis of one team's preference or an immediate need. What looks like local efficiency adds up to organizational drag, with decisions made without full context. The prescription is to treat platform choice as a single strategic decision, starting with an honest inventory of what is actually in use.
points: The piece claims collaboration tools can end up walling people off from one another when each team picks its own.
Ford's consolidation onto a single platform for about 170,000 employees is offered as evidence that unifying tools breaks down silos.
Each additional platform is described as an additional organizational boundary, however sensible it looks to the team that chose it.
Leaders are urged to make platform decisions centrally and begin by counting how many tools their organization really runs on.
quotes: Organizations often make expedient choices without thinking through the long-term implications of their decisions. Allowing competing communication channels to proliferate across the organization is a prime example.
Research on organizational silos consistently finds that teams relying on separate, unintegrated platforms interact less with one another.
The tools meant to help people work together end up doing the opposite.

Yet leaders often justify allowing multiple tools because a given team prefers a particular one or because that tool solves an immediate problem. But each additional platform creates an additional boundary.

What looks like local efficiency in each team adds up to organizational drag, where decisions are made without full context, priorities are set without full input, and varying work standards get applied haphazardly.
The task for leaders is to deal with platform proliferation as an overall strategic decision rather than a series of local ones.
